items.title: Half a Billion Christians Around the World Can’t Access the Bible, New Analysis Shows
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Concerning.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

While technology has greatly expanded the availability of Scripture, a perfect storm of calamities has kept the Bible out of the hands of half a billion Christians around the globe.

According to just-released data from the 2026 Bible Access List, the second such analysis from the Bible Access Initiative, 125 million believers are unable to access God’s Word in any format, even in countries where Scripture is technically allowed and safe to possess.

The report evaluates 106 countries and pinpoints where Christians face the greatest obstacles to accessing the Bible, some entirely and others in part.

“We often hear that the Bible is more accessible than ever, but we must not confuse availability with access,” Wybo Nicolai, co-founder of the Bible Access List, said in a statement about the latest data. “Persecution-related Bible access restrictions can make accessing Scripture difficult or dangerous, while socioeconomic barriers can put a Bible beyond people’s reach. Even where Scripture is available digitally, limited internet coverage or unsafe online environments can still prevent people from accessing it.”

Key barriers to access include persecution-related restrictions, social hostility toward Christians, threats from extremist groups, failing infrastructure, and socioeconomic issues, like poverty, lack of access to the internet, limited electricity, and illiteracy.

The top five countries on the coalition’s restrictions list (in order) are: Afghanistan, Yemen, Somalia, North Korea, and Eritrea.

“In Afghanistan, God’s Word is the most dangerous book any Afghan can possess,” the researchers stated. “And discovery can cost them their life. In North Korea, every dimension of Bible access is prohibited. Christians are treated as enemies of the state, and a Bible discovered in a routine house search can mean execution or a life sentence in a forced labor camp.”

The analysis looked at places, too, where believers don’t face legal restrictions but are suffering shortage of Bible access. Those top five countries (in order) are: the Democratic Republic of Congo (>10 million), Ethiopia (>10 million), Nigeria (>10 million), India (>10 million), and Uganda (5-10 million).

For context, there are more than 107 million Christians living in the DR Congo, but not even half — fewer than 33% — of believers there own a Bible in a country where it is legal to possess one.

“No law restricts access,” according to the report. “[But] the DRC is among the poorest countries in the world. Only about one in five people have electricity, and poor roads make remote communities difficult to reach in a country the size of Western Europe.”

items.title: Filmmaker Reveals What Charlie Kirk Said About Biblical Prophecy Before His Death
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "God's speaking to you."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Matthew Thayer’s new movie, “Can You Hear Me Now?” tackles biblical prophecy, exploring whether prophets still deliver messages to the masses today.

As part of the film, Thayer did one of the final interviews with conservative commentator Charlie Kirk before his assassination.

“I interviewed him with the impetus of talking to him about … the separation of church and state, Christian nationalism, all of the stuff that he was so eloquent at communicating,” Thayer said. “And it was a great interview.”

The filmmaker said he asked Kirk about prophecy and for his general take on whether it still occurs today.

“What he said blew me away,” said Thayer. “[Kirk’s] like, ‘Yeah, absolutely. I believe that there’s prophets, there’s prophecy — it’s a gift.’ It can be abused, but he’s seen it work and he’s seen it transform lives. But one of the things that he said that I thought was just right on was that a word from a prophet is not an excuse for … [inaction] or apathy.”

Kirk worried people might not have worked as hard as they could have in the 2020 election because they were relying on what they were told by a prophet and assumed it would be easily won.

“That actually, to me, points to a real fatalistic viewpoint that’s prevalent within the church of the will of God,” Thayer said. “That, if God speaks, it’s just going to happen. I don’t have to do anything about it. I can just pop some corn and sit on my couch and watch it all happen.”

Conversely, he said, a prophet’s role is to show up and alert people that situations are going the wrong way.

“A prophet’s word should be directional and actually require action upon the people and upon the people that are hearing it,” Thayer continued.

Ultimately, Thayer said he hopes “Can You Hear Me Now?” will inspire people to think deeper about how God might be speaking to them today.

“The biggest thing that was really kind of stuck with me the entire last year as we were making this film was all of the people that came out after Charlie Kirk’s death and were posting online going, ‘I’m being drawn to the Bible … Why do I want to go to church? I’m going to go to church’ — that was God speaking to all of those people.”

Thayer continued, “And so I really had a heart to really reach those people who are really infants in Christ and … kind of grab them by the collar and just go, ‘God’s speaking to you’ … because … there’s a whole swath of Christianity that doesn’t believe that God really kind of speaks.”

items.title: The Words on the Tip of Your Tongue
items.author: Jack F. Trent
items.summary:
Jack F. Trent

In order to truly fulfill our vocation, we must train our tongues with an eye to our good and our neighbor’s good, considered holistically.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Jack F. Trent

“I only killed one human being in Vietnam,” former US Marine John Musgraves says in a Vietnam War documentary. He continues,

And that was the first man that I ever killed. I was sick with guilt about killing that guy and thinking I’m going to have to do this for the next thirteen months—I’m going to go crazy. And then I saw a Marine step on a “bouncing betty” mine, and that’s when I made my deal with the devil in that I said I will never kill another human being as long as I’m in Vietnam. . . . “However, I will waste as many gooks as I can find. I’ll wax as many dinks as I can find. I’ll smoke as many zips as I can find. But I ain’t going to kill anybody.” 

Musgraves’s remorseful confession of his deceptive, euphemistic language reminds us that our words—whether spoken to oneself or to another—matter. Our words can lead us to life and communion, or they lead us to death and isolation—“Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov 18:21).

What Are Words?

The natural law dictates that a thing’s nature, or essence, determines its purpose. We cannot discern what X is for unless we know what X is. To give a concrete example, we know that a car is for transportation by observing what a car is—a box with wheels; and we can, moreover, determine if this car is good or bad by reference to its purpose. Does the car complete its purpose? That is, does the car transport well? If yes, then it is a good car; if not, then it is a bad car. This illustration is a rough outline of the natural law. 

Let us apply the natural law to our language. What are words? What is their nature? We can do lots of things with our vocal abilities—cough, cry, blow bubbles, etc.—but when we use our vocal abilities to signify (not just vaguely express), we are using words. Words are significant vocal sounds; they signify concepts of the intellect. 

A concept of the intellect (or mind) is a simple being of reason, such as the concept dog or animal. And because these simple concepts are immaterial, they can be in your intellect and my intellect at the same time. Purely material beings, on the other hand, cannot bilocate like so. We can combine our simple concepts of the intellect to make intellectual judgments, like dogs are animals. We can make these judgments known by our words in turn—“Dogs are animals.”

The way our words signify our concepts of the intellect is by means of a linguistic community. We are trained into a linguistic community; we are taught that the sound /dôg/ is used in this community to refer to this given thing—namely, the type of thing that has four legs and barks. There is not a universal, one-to-one relationship between a given word and its corresponding concept of the intellect. We can alter our vocal sounds and still signify the same concept of the intellect. This fact is why multiple languages can exist; table, mesa, and Tisch—quite distinct vocal sounds—can all signify the same concept of the intellect. Thus, Aristotle teaches, words are conventional vocal sounds. 

Indeed, society is the occasion for language. St. Thomas Aquinas, commenting on Aristotle, writes,

If man were by nature a solitary animal, the [concepts of the intellect] by which he was conformed to things to have knowledge of them would be sufficient for him; but since he is by nature a political and social animal, his conceptions had to be made known to others. He does this through vocal sound. Therefore, there had to be significant vocal sounds so that men might live together, and thus those who speak different languages find it difficult to live together in social unity.

Without society, we would not need words, and without words, society would not be possible. Language is a social phenomenon. Both Aquinas and Aristotle would be quick to remind us, however, that while words are conventional, our concepts of the intellect are not, for our concepts of the intellect are formed by reality, which offers itself the same to all human persons. 

Said another way, because we human persons are presented with the same world, we can form the same thoughts and thereby communicate in a spoken, intelligible manner. Thus, by engaging in conversation, we can enact true communion with our fellow man.

Above all, human communion via speech will entail a commitment to the truth, which is to say, a commitment to reality. Our intellects are made to know reality, and our words follow from our intellect. Any habit of verbally stretching or altering reality with the intention to deceive is therefore a violation of the way God constituted our being. Reality is the only place where true communion can occur.

Still, there is a way to utter true things that nevertheless leads to isolation and death (stating true mathematical facts at a weekend barbecue, or a funeral for that matter, will not get you any friends). In order to truly fulfill our vocation, we must train our tongues with an eye to our good and our neighbor’s good, considered holistically. 

Training the Tongue

Fr. Gregory Pine’s recent book Training the Tongue is an insightful manual aimed at leading us to become virtuous, communion-oriented speakers. Communion, for Fr. Pine, is the “fundamental goal of speech.” Indeed, man’s highest good is communion with God, and in this life “we cultivate communion with God through communion with our fellow man.” True happiness therefore entails a social—and hence, a linguistic—component. 

To achieve this end, Fr. Pine focuses on cultivating the virtues more so than on rooting out the vices. He reasons thus: If we want our souls to be like a beautiful garden, then the bulk of our time is not best spent on pulling out weeds (that is, rooting out sins), but rather on crowding out weeds by planting and tending good plants and flowers (that is, welcoming grace and cultivating the virtues). 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

Fr. Pine’s chapter titles testify to the diverse uses of speech: “Telling the Truth,” “Inquiring Together,” “Building Each Other Up,” “Offering Correction,” “Playing with Humor,” “Giving Instruction,” and “Talking to God.” At every juncture, Fr. Pine lets the reader know which virtues and vices are applicable to a particular speech genre. For example, the vice of indelicacy makes conversation unnecessarily uncomfortable and the virtue of humility ensures we do not speak too much about ourselves. Naming the relevant virtues and vices provides us with the clarity and precision needed to make progress. Above all, Fr. Pine highlights the importance of truthfulness: “The only thing sufficiently substantial to ground a worthy communal endeavor is reality itself.”

We need to cultivate a love for reality. Fr. Pine counsels us to live life in such a way that we “have plenty of good things to talk about,” for “if we take an interest in the world around us, we’ll have less difficulty cultivating a healthier vocal culture.” Experience confirms this: The best conversations are those centered around something true, good, or beautiful that transcends the interlocutors in conversation.  

Fr. Pine also encourages us to become genuinely interested in the person we are speaking to and to listen well. He writes, “The most important contribution you can make [to a conversation] is to listen well,” for the good listener “creates space for the [speaker] to flourish, confirming his goodness and accepting his vulnerability.” When it comes time for us to speak, Fr. Pine exhorts us to treat our contributions “as potential connections, not simply as ‘my turn.’”

Reflecting on the qualities of the virtuous speaker makes one realize that the speech of the saints must have been sublime. The saints knew that they were called—both naturally and supernaturally—to communion with God and with their neighbor. Their excellent speech followed from this vocation to love. Thus St. Thomas More was so pleasant to be around that King Henry would on occasion visit More’s house at Chelsea simply “to be merry with him.” St. Dominic Savio’s contemporaries “were anxious to become friendly and to converse with him.” St. Thérèse of Lisieux made her companions laugh while on her own death bed. It is not without reason that St. Josemaría Escrivá writes, “Every Christian has the duty to bring peace and joy to his own surroundings on earth,” and St. Francis de Sales teaches, “Unquestionably, faithful, straightforward sincere speech is a great ornament to the life of a Christian.”

Our Lord has told us we will render an account for every careless word we speak (see Matt 12:36). It is a Christian hope that such linguistic excellence is within our grasp. God has indeed furnished us with the means to achieve a well-trained tongue, though it may be a difficult, lifelong process—“Anyone who makes no mistakes in speaking is perfect, able to keep the whole body in check with a bridle.” (Jas 3:2). To this end, we owe a debt of gratitude to Fr. Gregory Pine, who has helped us in the process of training our tongues. Having read his book, I—for one—feel I have improved the words on the tip of my tongue, leading me closer to a life of communion and not death.

items.title: Ep 85 | ‘Introducing Communio Theology’— Tracey Rowland
items.author: Dr. Tod Worner
items.summary:
Dr. Tod Worner

Coming out of the Second Vatican Council, Communio theology reminded us that our faith is Christocentric - Christ centered.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Tod Worner

Coming out of the Second Vatican Council, there was a faction that saw the Council’s outcome as a tragic rupture with enduring tradition, while another faction seemed eager to declare a rupture with what were deemed outdated, if not ossified, ways. In the face of this, Communio theology emerged with figures like Hans Urs von Balthasar, Henri de Lubac, Romano Guardini, and Joseph Ratzinger (later Pope Benedict XVI) who reminded us that our faith is Christocentric — Christ-centered. Without this understanding, the center cannot hold. Tradition is nothing without Christ and reform is nothing without Christ. Join Dr. Tracey Rowland and me as we explore her compelling new book, Introducing Communio Theology on The Evangelization & Culture Podcast.
